title: Solitude is not escape
hookLine: being alone is for love of others, not away from them

cards: There are two ways to be alone in a room. One is loneliness: the phone that doesn't ring, the scroll through other people's lives, the sense of being left out. The other is different.
Someone shuts the door on purpose. The house goes quiet. And somehow the people they love come closer, not further away.
The first gets talked about all the time. The second hardly ever gets a name. Thomas Merton spent his last years alone in the woods, and he insisted he hadn't run away from anyone.

teach.b: First, the word. Solitude comes from the Latin solus, alone. But in the Christian tradition, being alone was never the point.
The desert hermits went out alone, and, the stories say, people came a long way to ask them for advice. Second, Merton's claim.

teach.h: NOT AWAY FROM PEOPLE, BUT FOR THEM.
teach.b: Across his books, Merton kept saying it: a person doesn't go into solitude to get away from people, but to learn how to love them better.
He warned that solitude chosen out of contempt for others, or to avoid them, is just loneliness with a nice name. Real solitude, he said, makes you more aware of your bond with everyone.
The hermit discovers he's carrying the whole world with him. Third, Jesus's pattern.
Luke says, in the Douay-Rheims: "And he retired into the desert, and prayed." Then he comes back, and the crowds are waiting.
Before he chose his twelve apostles, Luke says, he spent the whole night alone on a mountain in prayer. Solitude first, then people. Solitude for the people.
Fourth, the Catholic picture. Catholics believe prayer isn't private property.

teach.h: EVERY PRAYER JOINS THE WHOLE CHURCH.
teach.b: A monk in his cell, a grandmother with her rosary at midnight, a hermit in Kentucky: each prayer joins the prayer of the whole Church, and reaches people the one praying will never meet.
The Second Vatican Council said communities given wholly to contemplation hold a distinguished place in the Church.

how: Catholic contemplative monks and nuns, like Trappists and Carmelites, live largely hidden lives, and the Church teaches that their prayer serves the whole world; many lay Catholics make a holy hour of silent prayer for others.

games.q: you're a hermit, and someone says you've abandoned the world. what's Merton's answer?
o: I'm here to learn to love the world better
I'm here to rest from people
games.why: Merton kept saying real solitude isn't escape: it makes you more aware of your bond with everyone.

practice: Close your eyes or lower them, and notice that you're by yourself in this moment.

Then let three people come to mind, one at a time, holding each for a few breaths: someone you love, someone you find difficult, someone you've never met, a stranger in a hospital tonight, a kid somewhere scared.
If you pray, pray for each of them; if you don't, just wish them well.

wordCard.voice: Solitude. From the Latin for alone. For Merton, chosen quiet that doesn't flee people, but carries them, and learns to love them better. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: alone, for them. A quiet hour can carry other people in it. That's two hundred eighty-five.
